targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a thicket of slender, smooth, red-brown to grey stems sprouting from spreading roots, the crowns rounded and dense with dark green, pointed oval leaves; finger-long spikes of white flowers in late spring, drooping bunches of dark red to black cherries in late summer, leaves yellow to red in fall

description: A deciduous shrub or small tree, usually two to five metres, that spreads by its roots into thickets of slender, smooth, reddish-brown to grey stems. Its leaves are pointed ovals with finely toothed edges, dark green above and paler beneath. In late spring, after the leaves are out, it hangs with finger-long spikes of small white flowers that smell sweet and almond-like, and by late summer these become drooping bunches of shiny dark red to black cherries, puckeringly sour. In Grand Teton and Yellowstone it grows in the moist draws and ravines of the sagebrush hills, along streams, and at the edges of aspen groves, and its fruit is eaten by bears and many birds.

season_notes.winter: Bare red-brown and grey stems; mule deer and elk browse the twigs on their winter ranges.
season_notes.spring: Leaves open first, then white flower spikes in late May and June, their scent drifting across the draws.
season_notes.summer: Green cherries turn red and then nearly black by mid to late August; bears and birds come to the thickets.
season_notes.fall: Leaves turn yellow, orange and red; the last cherries drop or are eaten, and bears pass the stones.

riparian.water: Grows where the ground holds extra moisture: wooded draws, steep ravines, streambanks and terraces, spreading by root sprouts into thickets; it does not stand poor drainage or long flooding, and thins out on dry open slopes.

range.where: the draws, ravines and streambanks of the sagebrush hills of Jackson Hole and Yellowstone's northern range, and the edges of aspen groves and open Douglas-fir; across most of North America from the Atlantic to British Columbia and south to California and New Mexico

notes: The library has no Prunus; Saskatoon serviceberry (the template) is the nearest of the same family (Rosaceae) and leaf type (deciduous, simple, toothed, oval) and the same habit, a suckering multi-stemmed shrub to small tree of the same interior-West draws and aspen edges (itself a generated record, from toyon). Height 1-6 m, nearly 12 m in the Great Basin (FEIS); 1-6 m, rarely 10 m (Wikipedia); height_m 1.5-5 m is the drafter's for the Teton draws. Thicket-forming from rhizomes, numerous slender stems from the base (FEIS; Wikipedia: a suckering shrub or small tree). Leaves oval and pointed, serrated, 2.5-10 cm, dark green above and paler beneath (Wikipedia), hence leaf_size_m 0.07. Flowers white, fragrant, in racemes 4-11 cm (Wikipedia) on leafy twigs 1-3 weeks after leaf-out (FEIS), late May to mid-June in Montana (FEIS); the National Park Service Grand Teton trees and shrubs page names its fragrant early-summer bloom. The racemes and the hanging fruit are drawn through the generator's 'cluster' form (a 'raceme' form exists only in client/src/fruit.js); size_m 0.08 and 0.06 stand for a whole raceme. Fruit a drupe 6-14 mm, bright red to black (Wikipedia; the Rocky Mountain plants are the dark-fruited var. melanocarpa, the drafter's knowledge), ripe mid to late August in Montana (FEIS). Fall colour yellow to red is the drafter's judgement (Wikipedia gives it only for cultivars). Bark colour is the drafter's knowledge; no source read describes it. Habitat (FEIS): low to mid elevations with extra moisture, riparian areas, wooded draws and steep ravines, aspen stands, Douglas-fir and ponderosa pine types; shade tolerant but densest at forest edges; not tolerant of poor drainage or prolonged flooding; resprouts quickly from root crowns and rhizomes after fire (hence disturbed 1.2). No Wyoming elevation was read (FEIS gives Idaho 945-2440 m; its Montana figure, 177-225 m, is plainly an error); elev_m 1200-2600 m is the drafter's. The Teton placing (sagebrush steppe draws and aspen woodland) is from the brief. Eaters (FEIS): black and grizzly bears (fruit; they also spread the seed), elk (poor to good), mule deer (a preferred winter browse in the Intermountain West), moose, pronghorn, bighorn, white-tailed deer, many birds (fruit, nesting cover), snowshoe hares and porcupines; Wikipedia adds rabbits and notes the cyanogenic foliage and stones (wilted leaves dangerous to ruminants). Grizzly bear, moose, pronghorn, bighorn, white-tailed deer and porcupine are not in the library; the American robin stands in for the fruit-eating birds. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stems, lean, leaf-on months, habitat weights and the flower and fruit sizes are the drafter's judgement, not from a source. The FEIS URL under plants/shrub/ returned 404; the review is filed under plants/tree/.
